First read /tmp/AGENT_GUIDE.md carefully (rules + engine API). You work in a git worktree of /workspace (build with `cargo build --release` in your worktree root).

YOUR TASK: implement the `Temporal` global to match the ORIGINAL binary (which claims to pass test262 Temporal). You own `src/builtins/temporal.rs` (currently a stub; feel free to turn it into a directory module `src/builtins/temporal/mod.rs` with submodules). Keep the entry points `temporal::setup(vm)` and `temporal::instant_from_ms(vm, ms) -> JsResult<Value>` (used by Date.prototype.toTemporalInstant). Date math helpers exist in `src/datetime.rs` (civil date conversions, time zone data loaded from /usr/share/zoneinfo — read its docs); BigInt in `src/bigint.rs`.

Scope: Temporal.Now (instant, plainDateISO, plainDateTimeISO, plainTimeISO, zonedDateTimeISO, timeZoneId), Temporal.Instant, PlainDate, PlainTime, PlainDateTime, PlainYearMonth, PlainMonthDay, ZonedDateTime, Duration — constructors, `from` (ISO 8601 / RFC 9557 string parsing with brackets/annotations, property bags with overflow constrain/reject), getters, `with`, add/subtract, until/since with largestUnit/smallestUnit/roundingIncrement/roundingMode, round, equals, compare, toString with options (fractionalSecondDigits, smallestUnit, calendarName, timeZoneName, offset), toJSON, toLocaleString (via datetime.rs formatting if possible), valueOf throwing TypeError, conversions (toPlainDate, toZonedDateTime, ...), Duration.total/round/balance/negated/abs/sign/blank, Symbol.toStringTag values ("Temporal.PlainDate" etc.). Calendars: ISO 8601 ("iso8601") at minimum; check which others the original supports. Time zones: UTC, fixed offsets and IANA names via datetime.rs.

Probe the original extensively (typical usage first: Temporal.PlainDate.from('2024-03-15').add({months: 1}).toString(), durations between dates, Temporal.Now..., ZonedDateTime with 'America/New_York', round, compare), then edge cases and exact error messages (RangeError/TypeError texts). Write comparison scripts in /tmp/temporalagent/ and iterate until outputs match the original byte-for-byte. Commit in your worktree branch. Final reply: branch/commit, what's done, known differences, core-engine bugs found (with JS repro).

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

# Guide for subagents working on the lumen reimplementation

## The project
We are reimplementing, from scratch in Rust (std only, NO external crates), a JavaScript engine +
Node/Bun-like runtime called "lumen" (CLI `lumen-cli`). The ORIGINAL compiled binary is at
`/workspace/executable` (symlink `/tmp/orig`). Our reimplementation lives in the git repo `/workspace`
(you will be working in your own git worktree copy of it). Hidden tests will run JS programs through
both binaries and compare stdout, stderr and exit code EXACTLY, so fidelity to the original's
observable behavior (output formats, error messages, property orders, edge cases) is the goal.

## Rules (strict)
- You may RUN the original (`/tmp/orig file.js`, `/tmp/orig -e 'code'`) to observe behavior.
- You MUST NOT disassemble/decompile/read the original binary's bytes, use strace/ltrace/gdb on it,
  search the internet, or download anything. No network is available anyway.
- Do not copy JS source code text of the original's internal modules verbatim (some functions print
  their JS source via `String(fn)`; you may observe *behavior*, but write your own Rust implementation).
- Write Rust (std only). Keep any scratch scripts (shell/python/JS test files) OUTSIDE the repo, e.g.
  under `/tmp/<yourname>/`. Do not add non-Rust code files to the repo.
- Only edit the files assigned to you. If a core-engine bug blocks you, work around it in your files
  if possible and describe the bug precisely in your final report (file/function, repro JS). If you
  absolutely must touch a shared file, keep the change minimal and list it in your report.
- Never run `/workspace/compile.sh` and never write to `/workspace/executable`.
- Build with `cargo build --release` in YOUR worktree (binary: `target/release/lumen`). Commit your
  work in your worktree with clear messages when done (and at milestones).
- `console.log` in lumen prints values via `String(v)` (objects print as `[object Object]`), so when
  probing the original use JSON.stringify or explicit string building.

## Engine architecture (what you need to write builtins)
Key modules (in `src/`): `value.rs` (Value, JsStr, Sym, PropKey), `object.rs` (Obj, ObjKind, Prop,
PropDesc, Args, NativeFn, flags WRITABLE/ENUMERABLE/CONFIGURABLE, WEC, WC), `vm.rs` (Vm, JsResult,
calls, errors, frames, Job), `props.rs` (property internal methods on Vm), `ops.rs` (conversions),
`realm.rs` (intrinsics + helpers to define builtins), `builtins/*` (ECMAScript builtins),
`runtime/*` (node/web runtime), `runtime/mod.rs` (Host state, event loop), `modules.rs` (ESM).

### Values
```rust
enum Value { Undefined, Null, Bool(bool), Num(f64), Str(JsStr), Sym(Sym), BigInt(Rc<BigInt>), Obj(Obj), Empty /*internal*/ }
JsStr::from_str("x"), s.to_rust_string(), s.units() -> &[u16] (UTF-16), JsStr::from_units(vec), JsStr::concat(&a,&b)
Value::str("x"), Value::Num(1.0), v.is_undefined(), v.is_nullish(), v.as_obj() -> Option<&Obj>, v.truthy(), v.is_callable()
PropKey::from_str("name"), PropKey::Str(js), PropKey::Sym(sym), PropKey::from_index(i)
```
### Natives
```rust
type NativeFn = fn(&mut Vm, &Args) -> JsResult<Value>;   // JsResult<T> = Result<T, Value /*thrown*/>
// Args: a.this (Value), a.args (&[Value]), a.arg(i) -> Value (undefined if missing), a.callee (&Obj),
//       a.new_target (Option<Obj>, Some when called with `new`), a.slot(i) -> captured data (see native_closure)
vm.native_fn("name", length, f) -> Obj                         // function object
vm.native_closure("name", length, f, vec![slot0, slot1]) -> Obj // with captured Values (read via a.slot(i))
vm.def_method(&obj, "name", length, f) -> Obj                    // non-enumerable writable configurable method
vm.def_getter(&obj, "name", f); vm.def_accessor(&obj, "name", getter, setter)
vm.native_ctor("Name", length, f, &proto) -> Obj   // constructor; links proto.constructor & ctor.prototype
// In a constructor native: let p = vm.proto_from_nt(&a.new_target, &fallback_proto)?; Obj::new(Some(p), kind)
vm.make_ctor(&fobj)  // mark a native fn as constructible
vm.def_global("Name", Value::Obj(o)); vm.set_tag(&obj, "Tag") // Symbol.toStringTag
```
### Objects
```rust
vm.new_object() -> Obj (plain, Object.prototype); vm.obj_from(vec![("k", v), ...]) -> Obj (enumerable props)
vm.new_array(vec![...]) -> Obj; Obj::new(proto: Option<Obj>, ObjKind::Ordinary)
o.set_str("k", v, WEC); o.set_prop(PropKey, v, flags); o.get_own_str("k") -> Option<Value> (own data only)
o.borrow() / o.borrow_mut()  (RefCell — never hold a borrow across a call into JS!)
// custom native state: Obj::new(Some(proto), ObjKind::Host(Box::new(MyState{..}))) and later
//   if let ObjKind::Host(h) = &o.borrow().kind { if let Some(s) = h.downcast_ref::<MyState>() {..} }
//   (use Cell/RefCell inside MyState for mutation)
crate::runtime::reorder_enum(vm, &obj, &["a","b",...]) // force enumerable key order (missing -> noop fns)
```
### Property access / conversions (all on `vm`)
```rust
vm.get(&obj, &key, &receiver_value)?; vm.get_str(&obj, "name")?; vm.get_prop_of(&value, &key)? (works on primitives)
vm.set_prop_of(&value, key, v, /*strict*/ true)?; vm.create_data_property(&obj, key, v)?
vm.has_property(&obj, &key)?; vm.delete(&obj, &key)?; vm.own_property_keys(&obj)?; vm.enumerable_own_keys(&obj)?
vm.to_string(&v)? -> JsStr; vm.to_number(&v)?; vm.to_object(&v)?; vm.to_property_key(&v)?; vm.to_index(&v)?
vm.to_integer_or_infinity(&v)?; vm.to_int32/to_uint32; vm.to_primitive(&v, crate::ops::Hint::Default)?
crate::runtime::display_value(vm, &v) -> String   // what console.log prints for a value
crate::runtime::util::inspect_value(vm, &v, depth)? -> String  // util.inspect
crate::runtime::util::describe_received(vm, &v) -> String // Node-style "Received type number (5)"
vm.call(&f, this, &args)?; vm.construct(&ctor, &args, None)?; vm.iterate_to_vec(&iterable)?
crate::builtins::array::array_like_to_vec(vm, &v)?
```
### Errors
```rust
return vm.throw_type("message");   // also throw_range, throw_ref, throw_syntax, throw_error("URIError", msg)
let e = vm.make_error("TypeError", "msg"); if let Value::Obj(o) = &e { o.set_prop(PropKey::from_str("code"), Value::str("ERR_X"), WEC); } return Err(e);
```
### Promises / async / event loop
```rust
let cap = vm.new_promise_capability_intrinsic(); // Capability { promise, resolve, reject }
vm.call(&cap.resolve, Value::Undefined, &[v])?; return Ok(cap.promise);
crate::builtins::promise::promise_then(vm, &promise_obj, on_fulfilled_fn_value, on_rejected_fn_value)?
crate::builtins::promise::perform_then_internal(vm, &p, Handler::Native(f, data), Handler::Native(g, data), None)
   // f: fn(&mut Vm, Value /*result*/, &Value /*data*/) -> JsResult<Value>
vm.jobs.push_back(crate::vm::Job::Callback(f, args));      // microtask
vm.host.callbacks.push_back((f, args));                     // macrotask (setImmediate-like queue)
crate::runtime::timers::add_timer(vm, cb, delay_ms, args, repeat) -> id
crate::runtime::spawn_op(vm, move || { /* runs on a thread, return T: Send */ }, move |vm, t: T| { /* back on loop thread */ });
   // keeps the event loop alive until `then` runs. Never move Values/Objs into the thread closure.
```
### Buffers / bytes
```rust
crate::runtime::buffer::new_buffer_value(vm, bytes)?      // Node Buffer (Uint8Array subclass)
crate::runtime::buffer::bytes_of(vm, &v)?                  // bytes of string(utf8)/Buffer/TypedArray/ArrayBuffer/array
crate::builtins::typedarray::ta_bytes(&obj)                // bytes of TypedArray/ArrayBuffer/DataView
crate::builtins::typedarray::typed_array_from_bytes(vm, bytes) -> Obj  // plain Uint8Array
crate::runtime::buffer::{encode_string, decode_bytes, norm_encoding}   // node encodings
crate::runtime::encoding::{base64_encode, base64_decode_strict, hex_encode, utf16_to_utf8, utf8_to_utf16}
```
### EventEmitter helpers
`crate::runtime::events::{install_methods(vm,&proto), init_emitter(vm,&obj), emit_event(vm,&this_value,&Value::str("evt"),&args)?}`
and `create_module(vm)` returns the EventEmitter constructor (also cached via `crate::runtime::node::builtin_module(vm, "events")?`).

### Module registry
`crate::runtime::node::builtin_module(vm, "name")? -> Option<Value>` returns (cached) exports of a node
builtin (used by `require`, `import`, `process.getBuiltinModule`). The dispatch is in
`runtime/node.rs::builtin_module`; your module's `create_module(vm, name)` is already wired.
Globals are installed by `setup(vm)` functions called from `runtime/mod.rs::setup_runtime`.

## Testing
Write JS test files under `/tmp/<yourname>/` and compare outputs of `/tmp/orig` vs your build:
`/tmp/orig t.js > o1 2> e1; echo $? ; target/release/lumen t.js > o2 2> e2; echo $?; diff o1 o2; diff e1 e2`.
Cover typical usage first (what a test-writer would exercise), then edge cases and error messages.
Note process.argv[0]/timings legitimately differ.

- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

// Temporal (minimal subset).

use crate::object::*;
use crate::value::*;
use crate::vm::{JsResult, Vm};

pub fn setup(vm: &mut Vm) {
    let t = vm.new_object();
    let now = vm.new_object();
    vm.def_method(&now, "instant", 0, now_instant);
    vm.set_tag(&now, "Temporal.Now");
    t.set_prop(PropKey::from_str("Now"), Value::Obj(now), WC);
    vm.set_tag(&t, "Temporal");
    vm.def_global("Temporal", Value::Obj(t));
}

fn now_instant(vm: &mut Vm, _a: &Args) -> JsResult<Value> {
    instant_from_ms(vm, crate::datetime::now_ms())
}

pub fn instant_from_ms(vm: &mut Vm, t: f64) -> JsResult<Value> {
    if t.is_nan() {
        return vm.throw_range("Invalid time value");
    }
    let o = vm.new_object();
    o.set_str("epochMilliseconds", Value::Num(t), WEC);
    Ok(Value::Obj(o))
}

1://! `Date` support for the lumen runtime: ECMA-262 time-value algorithms,
2://! the fixed string formats, `Date.parse` / `new Date(string)` parsing and
3://! the locale-sensitive formatting behind `toLocaleString` & co. (an
4://! `Intl.DateTimeFormat` subset).  Pure std, no unsafe.
5://!
6://! Everything below was established by black-box observation of the original
7://! `lumen` binary (differential tests over ~11k timestamps/argument tuples,
8://! ~65k parse strings and ~80k locale/option/time-zone cases all agree).
9://!
10://! # Local time zone
11://! The original ALWAYS uses UTC as its local time zone: `TZ` is ignored,
12://! `getTimezoneOffset()` is 0 and `toString()` ends in
13://! `GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)`.  [`local_tza`] is therefore 0 and
14://! [`local_time`] / [`utc`] are identities.
15://!
16://! # String formats
17://! * `toString`: `"Thu Jan 01 1970 00:00:00 GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)"`
18://! * `toDateString`: `"Thu Jan 01 1970"`, `toTimeString`: `"00:00:00 GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)"`
19://! * `toUTCString` (== `toGMTString`): `"Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT"`
20://! * Years in these three: at least 4 digits, sign for negatives:
21://!   `-0001`, `0000`, `0999`, `12345`, `-271821`, `275760`.
22://! * `toISOString`: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ`, years outside 0..=9999 as
23://!   `+275760` / `-000001` (6 digits + sign).  NaN: the caller throws
24://!   `RangeError: Invalid time value` (same message for `Intl` formatting of
25://!   an invalid time).  `toJSON` of an invalid date gives `null`.
26://! * All of them give `"Invalid Date"` for NaN (`String(new Date(NaN))`,
27://!   `new Date(8.64e15 + 1)`); the toLocale* family too.
28://! * Calling a Date method on a non-Date: `TypeError: this is not a Date object`.
29://!
30://! # Constructor / setters (caller side)
31://! * `new Date(y, m, ...)`, `Date.UTC` and `setYear` map years 0..=99 (after
32://!   ToIntegerOrInfinity) to 1900+y; that is the caller's job.  `Date.UTC()`
33://!   with no argument is NaN; `Date.UTC(2020)` = month 0.
34://! * [`make_day`] returns NaN when `year + floor(month / 12)` is outside
35://!   ±300000 (the original's limit; V8 uses ±1e6), otherwise exact f64 math.
36://! * Setters on an invalid date: per spec (`setFullYear`, `setUTCFullYear`
37://!   and Annex B `setYear` start from +0, the others stay NaN).
38://!   [`time_clip`] turns -0 into +0.
39://!
40://! # Parsing
41://! `Date.parse(s)` ([`parse`]) tries, in order:
42://! 1. **Strict ISO** ([`parse_iso`]), after Rust `str::trim` (Unicode
43://!    White_Space, so U+FEFF is *not* trimmed):
44://!    `YYYY | ±YYYYYY` (`-000000` rejected) `[-MM[-DD]]`
45://!    `[T HH[:mm[:ss]][.f+][Z | ±HH:mm]]`.  Fields are not range-checked
46://!    (`2020-13-01` = 2021-01-01, `2020-02-30` = 2020-03-01, `T24:00:01`,
47://!    `T25:00`, offsets `+99:99` all accepted); hour-only `T10` and
48://!    fractions after hour/minute (`T10.5`) are fine; 1+ fraction digits,
49://!    truncated to ms.  Lowercase `t`/`z`, `+0100`, `+01` are rejected.
50://!    Date-only = UTC, date-time without offset = local (= UTC).
51://! 2. **Space-separated variant** (only when the string contains a U+0020):
52://!    split at the first space; date `[+|-]Y+[-M{1,2}[-D{1,2}]]` (any number
53://!    of year digits), time `H{1,2}[:m{1,2}[:s{1,2}]][.f+]` followed by `Z` or
54://!    an offset introduced by the LAST `+`/`-`: `±HH`, `±HHMM` or `±HH:MM`.
55://!    So `"2020-1-2 3:4"`, `"202 03:04"`, `"2020-01-02 03:04:05+0100"` parse
56://!    although the ISO path rejects them.
57://! 3. **Legacy tokens** ([`parse_legacy`], see its docs): month names by
58://!    their first three letters, numbers assigned to day/year by magnitude,
59://!    first `h:m:s` token = time, `GMT±hhmm` / signed tokens = offsets;
60://!    AM/PM and zone abbreviations are IGNORED; parentheses are separators,
61://!    not comments; no two-digit-year mapping; computed with wrapping i64
62://!    arithmetic and **not TimeClip'ed** (`Date.parse("Sep 14 275760")` is
63://!    8640000086400000).
64://!
65://! `new Date(string)` ([`parse_for_constructor`]) only uses 1. and 2.:
66://! legacy strings — even the original's own `toString()` output — give an
67://! Invalid Date there, while `Date.parse` accepts them.
68://!
69://! Where the original *panics* (aborting the process: a non-ASCII character
70://! inside a 4-byte `±HHMM` offset of the space-separated form, e.g.
71://! `"2376 x-5é("`) this module returns NaN.
72://!
73://! # Locale formatting (`toLocaleString`, `Intl.DateTimeFormat`)
74://! The original has a small built-in `Intl` with its own patterns, not CLDR:
75://! * Default: `"1/1/1970, 12:00:00 AM"` (toLocaleString), `"1/1/1970"`,
76://!   `"12:00:00 AM"`; the default locale is `en`, time zone `UTC`.
77://! * Locale data exists for ar de en es fr gv hi it ja ko ln nl pl pt ru si
78://!   sl sr sv th zh (zh-TW/HK/MO use Traditional names; ar-MA/DZ/TN/LY/EH/MR
79://!   use latn digits); any other language falls back to `en`.  Only the
80://!   numeric date order/separator (`3/7/2020`, `7.3.2020`, `7/3/2020`,
81://!   `2020/3/7`, `7-3-2020`, `2020-3-7`), month and era names, default hour
82://!   cycle (h12 for en, h23 otherwise; hour12 => h11 for ja) and digits
83://!   (ar => arab) are localised.  Weekday names, AM/PM, day periods and
84://!   time-zone names are always English; textual dates always use the
85://!   English layout (`"Saturday, März 7, 2020"` for de).
86://! * Pattern: `[weekday ", "] date-body [" " era] [", " time] [" " tzName]`
87://!   where the body is `month[" " day][", " year]` for textual months
88://!   (`"Mar, 2020"`, `"March 7"`) or the locale's numeric order joined by its
89://!   separator; time = `h:mm:ss` of the present fields (minutes and seconds
90://!   always 2-digit, hour 2-digit in h23/h24 unless a dayPeriod is shown),
91://!   `.fff` fractional seconds (appended directly when no seconds), then
92://!   ` AM`/` PM` for h11/h12 or the English day period
93://!   (`in the morning`, `noon`/`n`, `in the afternoon`, `in the evening`,
94://!   `at night`).  `{weekday:"long"}` alone gives `"Saturday, "`.
95://! * Styles: dateStyle full/long/medium/short = weekday+long month / long
96://!   month / short month / numeric with 2-digit year; timeStyle full/long add
97://!   the long/short zone name.  Mixing styles with explicit components:
98://!   `TypeError: dateStyle/timeStyle cannot be combined with explicit date-time components`.
99://! * Errors: `RangeError: invalid <option>: <value>`,
100://!   `RangeError: fractionalSecondDigits out of range`,
101://!   `RangeError: invalid time zone: <name>`,
102://!   `RangeError: Incorrect locale information provided: <tag>`,
103://!   `TypeError: options must be an object` (non-object, non-undefined
104://!   options), `TypeError: locale must be a string or object` (bad list
105://!   element), `TypeError: Cannot convert null to object` (locales = null).
106://! * Option read order (spec order): localeMatcher, calendar,
107://!   numberingSystem, hour12, hourCycle, timeZone, weekday, era, year,
108://!   month, day, dayPeriod, hour, minute, second, fractionalSecondDigits,
109://!   timeZoneName, formatMatcher, dateStyle, timeStyle.  String options use
110://!   ToString, hour12 ToBoolean, fractionalSecondDigits ToNumber.  An invalid
111://!   date returns "Invalid Date" before locales/options are even read.
112://! * Calendars: gregory/iso8601, buddhist, roc and japanese are implemented;
113://!   the other calendars the original supports (islamic*, chinese, dangi,
114://!   hebrew, persian, indian, coptic, ethiopic, ethioaa) are reported in
115://!   resolvedOptions but formatted as Gregorian (known gap).
116://! * Numbering systems: all decimal systems (`-u-nu-` or the option).
117://!
118://! # Time zones
119://! `UTC` (any case), offsets `±HH`, `±HHMM`, `±HH:MM` (resolved as `±HH:MM`)
120://! and every IANA name of the system tz database (case-insensitive,
121://! canonical case returned, links keep their own name) read at runtime from
122://! `/usr/share/zoneinfo` (TZif + `tzdata.zi`).  Quirks reproduced:
123://! * no DST after 2037 (the original's data ends there);
124://! * `timeZoneName` short/shortOffset/shortGeneric = `GMT±h[:mm]` of the
125://!   offset in effect at the EPOCH, not at the formatted date
126://!   (`America/New_York` in July is still `GMT-5`); `UTC` => `UTC`;
127://! * long names: a few CLDR names (Eastern/Central/Mountain/Pacific
128://!   Standard Time, India/Japan/China Standard Time, Central European
129://!   Standard Time, Coordinated Universal Time) else a representative zone
130://!   id (`Europe/London` => `Europe/Guernsey`) — embedded table;
131://! * zones that are links in the original's (non-backzone) data use the
132://!   link target's history; the 2026 rule changes for Morocco and
133://!   Alberta/Manitoba that the original lacks are undone.
135://!
136://! # API overview (for the JS bindings)
137://! * time math: [`day`], [`time_within_day`], [`days_in_year`],
138://!   [`day_from_year`], [`time_from_year`], [`year_from_time`],
139://!   [`in_leap_year`], [`month_from_time`], [`date_from_time`], [`week_day`],
140://!   [`hour_from_time`], [`min_from_time`], [`sec_from_time`],
141://!   [`ms_from_time`], [`make_time`], [`make_day`], [`make_date`],
142://!   [`time_clip`], [`local_tza`], [`local_time`], [`utc`], [`now_ms`],
143://!   [`fields`] (all UTC fields at once).
144://! * strings: [`to_date_string`], [`to_date_only_string`],
145://!   [`to_time_only_string`], [`to_iso_string`], [`to_utc_string`].
146://! * parsing: [`parse`] (`Date.parse`, result NOT clipped),
147://!   [`parse_for_constructor`] (`new Date(str)`, already clipped).
148://! * locale: build a [`DateTimeFormatOptions`] (`set`, `set_hour12`,
149://!   `set_fractional_second_digits`), call [`canonicalize_locale_list`]
150://!   first (its error must win over option errors), then
151://!   [`to_locale_string`] / [`to_locale_date_string`] /
152://!   [`to_locale_time_string`] or [`DateTimeFormat`] (`new`, `format`,
153://!   `format_to_parts`, `resolved_options`) and [`supported_locales_of`].
154://!   Errors are [`DateTimeError`] { kind: Range | Type, message }.

import sys
def load(cal):
    rows = []
    for part in ['_a', '', '_b']:
        txt = open(f'/tmp/temporalagent/tab_{cal}{part}.txt').read().strip()
        for r in txt.split(';'):
            a, b, c, d = map(int, r.split(','))
            rows.append((a, b, c, d))
    return rows

B64 = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/'
out = {}
for cal in ['chinese', 'dangi']:
    rows = load(cal)
    first_year = -1000
    # consistency
    for i in range(len(rows) - 1):
        start, miy, mask, leap = rows[i]
        total = sum(30 if mask >> k & 1 else 29 for k in range(miy))
        if rows[i + 1][0] - start != total:
            print('inconsistent', cal, first_year + i, rows[i + 1][0] - start, total, file=sys.stderr)
        if (leap != 0) != (miy == 13):
            print('leap/miy mismatch', cal, first_year + i, file=sys.stderr)
    # encode: start delta vs mean year
    s = []
    base = rows[0][0]
    maxd = 0
    for i, (start, miy, mask, leap) in enumerate(rows):
        approx = base + round(i * 365.2422)
        delta = start - approx
        maxd = max(maxd, abs(delta))
        v = ((delta + 64) & 127) | (mask << 7) | (leap << 20)
        s.append(B64[v >> 18 & 63] + B64[v >> 12 & 63] + B64[v >> 6 & 63] + B64[v & 63])
    print(cal, 'maxdelta', maxd, 'base', base, 'years', len(rows), file=sys.stderr)
    out[cal] = (base, ''.join(s))

with open('/tmp/temporalagent/cn_tables.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write('// Generated from observed behaviour of the original (years -1000..=4000).\n')
    f.write('pub const LUNISOLAR_FIRST_YEAR: i64 = -1000;\n')
    for cal in ['chinese', 'dangi']:
        base, s = out[cal]
        f.write(f'pub const {cal.upper()}_BASE: i64 = {base};\n')
        f.write(f'pub const {cal.upper()}_DATA: &str = concat!(\n')
        for i in range(0, len(s), 96):
            f.write(f'    "{s[i:i+96]}",\n')
        f.write(');\n')

import json, sys
d = json.load(open('/tmp/temporalagent/l4_o.json'))
units = ['years', 'months', 'weeks', 'days', 'hours', 'minutes', 'seconds', 'milliseconds', 'microseconds', 'nanoseconds']
ns = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 11, 12, 21, 22, 25, 100, 101, 102, 111, 1000, 1001, 1002, 1000000]
AR = '٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩'

def digits_of(loc):
    return AR if loc == 'ar' else '0123456789'

def fmt_num(n, loc, group):
    s = str(n)
    out = ''
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        if i > 0 and (len(s) - i) % 3 == 0:
            out += group
        out += c
    dg = digits_of(loc)
    return ''.join(dg[int(c)] if c.isdigit() else c for c in out)

def group_sep(loc, s1000):
    dg = digits_of(loc)
    one = dg[1]
    zero = dg[0]
    # find separator between first digit and '000'
    i = s1000.index(one)
    j = s1000.index(zero * 3, i)
    return s1000[i + 1:j]

locales = {}
problems = 0
for loc in d:
    L = {}
    group = group_sep(loc, d[loc]['short']['years'][14])
    L['group'] = group
    for st in ['short', 'long', 'narrow']:
        S = {}
        for u in units:
            arr = d[loc][st][u]
            one_s = arr[0]
            n1 = fmt_num(1, loc, group)
            one_p = one_s.replace(n1, '{0}', 1) if n1 in one_s else one_s
            n2 = fmt_num(2, loc, group)
            other_p = arr[1].replace(n2, '{0}', 1)
            # verify
            for n, s in zip(ns, arr):
                p = one_p if n == 1 else other_p
                exp = p.replace('{0}', fmt_num(n, loc, group))
                if exp != s:
                    print('MISMATCH', loc, st, u, n, repr(s), repr(exp), file=sys.stderr)
                    problems += 1
            S[u] = (one_p, other_p)
        # lists
        x = d[loc][st]
        def label(u, n):
            p = S[u][0] if n == 1 else S[u][1]
            return p.replace('{0}', fmt_num(n, loc, group))
        a, b, c, e = label('days', 4), label('hours', 5), label('minutes', 6), label('seconds', 7)
        l2 = x['list2']
        pair = l2[len(b):len(l2) - len(c)]
        assert l2.startswith(b) and l2.endswith(c), (loc, st, l2)
        l3 = x['list3']
        # b MID c END e
        rest = l3[len(b):]
        mid = None
        for k in range(len(rest)):
            if rest[k:].startswith(c):
                mid = rest[:k]
                rest2 = rest[k + len(c):]
                end = rest2[:len(rest2) - len(e)]
                break
        l4 = x['list4']
        exp4 = a + mid + b + mid + c + end + e
        if exp4 != l4:
            print('LIST4 MISMATCH', loc, st, repr(l4), repr(exp4), file=sys.stderr)
            problems += 1
        S['list'] = (pair, mid, end)
        L[st] = S
    locales[loc] = L
print('problems', problems, file=sys.stderr)
json.dump(locales, open('/tmp/temporalagent/durdata.json', 'w'), ensure_ascii=False, indent=0)

content.text:
I've implemented the full `Temporal` global, and randomized differential testing against the original (tens of thousands of generated cases) now produces identical output for everything except the gaps listed below. All work is committed on branch `worktree-agent-a627be2e223307580`; HEAD is `5c65db3`, 10 commits on top of `08ab09b`. `cargo build --release` is clean and the Temporal code has no warnings.

**What's done**
- `src/builtins/temporal.rs` is now a directory module (`src/builtins/temporal/`, about 9.8k lines). `setup(vm)` and `instant_from_ms(vm, ms)` keep their signatures.
- **Types:** everything the original exposes — Now (`instant`, `timeZoneId`, `zonedDateTimeISO`, `plainDateISO`, `plainTimeISO`, `plainDateTimeISO`), Instant, PlainDate, PlainTime, PlainDateTime, PlainYearMonth, PlainMonthDay, ZonedDateTime and Duration. Constructors, `from`/`compare`, getters, `with`, add/subtract, until/since with all rounding options, round, total, equals, the conversions, `getTimeZoneTransition`, toString/toJSON options, `toLocaleString`, and `valueOf` throwing are all there.
- **API surface:** property order, `name`/`length`, attributes and `Symbol.toStringTag` match the original. Getters are named `year`, not `get year`, like the original.
- **Parsing:** full ISO 8601 / RFC 9557 grammar with annotations and critical flags.
- **Error messages:** the original's exact messages, including the many per-type variants (e.g. "UTC designator not valid for PlainDate", "no time in PlainTime string", "date-time outside representable range" vs "…is outside the representable range").
- **Original's quirks reproduced:**
  - It deviates from the spec in a few date-difference cases, e.g. `2024-03-31 until 2024-02-29` is `-P31D`, not `-P1M`.
  - It also differs from the spec in when it rounds up past the end of a month.
  - `ZonedDateTime.toString` rounds wall-clock time, and `toJSON` keeps second-precision offsets.
  - Bags fall back to `iso8601` when given Temporal objects.
  - `PlainMonthDay.toPlainDate` uses the ISO reference day for non-ISO calendars.
  - Plus various option-reading orders.
- **Calendars:** iso8601, gregory, japanese, buddhist, roc, hebrew, chinese, dangi, islamic-civil/-tbla/-umalqura, persian, indian, coptic, ethiopic and ethioaa, with eras, aliases and month codes. Chinese/dangi (years -1010..4010) and Umm al-Qura (AH 1300–1600) use data tables taken from the original's own output.
- **Time zones:** UTC, minute-precision offsets, and IANA names via `datetime.rs`. Link names are preserved but compare equal (e.g. `US/Eastern` equals `America/New_York`).
- **toLocaleString:** date/time types go through `datetime.rs` with the original's component filtering and errors. `Duration` has a DurationFormat implementation with the original's data for 15 locales.

**Shared file changed:** `src/datetime.rs` — I appended one `impl TimeZone` block with three read-only accessors used by Temporal (`primary_id`, `next_offset_transition`, `prev_offset_transition`). Nothing existing was modified.

**Known differences**
1. `toLocaleString` with a non-Gregorian formatter calendar (e.g. `{calendar: 'hebrew'}`) prints Gregorian numbers; the original prints `Adar I 25, 5784`. This is a gap in `datetime.rs` and `Date.prototype.toLocaleString` has it too. Once that file supports calendars, Temporal follows automatically; the calendar conversions in `temporal::calendar`/`cals` could be reused for it.
2. `new Intl.DateTimeFormat().format(temporalObject)` throws (valueOf TypeError) in ours; the original formats it. A proper fix needs `intl.rs` to keep the raw DateTimeFormat options, so I didn't touch it.
3. Chinese/dangi dates outside 1010 BCE–4010 CE use an approximation. The original's own results there are broken (negative month numbers), and its chinese `until` over about 100 years takes over 60 seconds.
4. America/Bogota's 1992 DST start is one day off (May 2 vs May 3). This comes from the system tz data in `datetime.rs`, not from Temporal.

**Core-engine issues found (not Temporal)**
- Arrow functions in stack traces: `try { [1].map(() => { throw new Error("x"); }); } catch (e) { console.log(e.stack) }` prints `at <anonymous>` in the original but `at anonymous` in ours.
- `structuredClone` is not defined in ours (`structuredClone({})` throws ReferenceError); the original has it.
- `Intl.DurationFormat`, `Intl.Locale`, `Intl.DisplayNames` and `Intl.Segmenter` are missing from ours.

The probe and randomized comparison scripts are in `/tmp/temporalagent/`; `regress.sh` there re-runs the whole suite.
